stories.nickname: The twenty minutes on the door
stories.situation: Luana had a class of 32 eight-year-olds, and no one in the school could say how well any of them read. The state literacy test came round every other year and the results arrived long after the children had moved up a year. She started a reading slot of 20 minutes at the beginning of every day and, because nothing existed to measure it with, began timing each child reading aloud every fortnight and writing the count in a school exercise book.
stories.stakes: Her diretora thought the slot was 20 minutes taken off maths, and said so at a staff meeting. If the reading figures had not moved, the slot would have been the first thing cut when the timetable was redone, and Luana would have had nothing to argue with but her own impression of the children.
actions: Timed every child reading aloud for one minute every fortnight and wrote the words-per-minute count next to their name, 24 rounds of it in the end, filling 2 exercise books
Grouped the children by where they actually were rather than by age, and changed the groups every month from the counts rather than from how the lessons felt
Sat with the four slowest readers herself during the slot and gave the rest to pairs, so the slot did not need a second adult
Took the exercise books to the staff meeting and read out the March and December averages rather than defending the idea
Wrote the timing method on one side of paper so another teacher could run it without being trained
stories.result: The class average went from 41 words read aloud per minute in March to 78 in December. The slot was adopted by all 14 classes the following year. The district's pedagogical team asked for her one-page method and now sends it out to new teachers.
stories.reflection: She had kept the counts for herself, not to prove anything, and it was only when the slot was about to be cut that she understood she was holding the only evidence in the building. She writes things down now expecting to have to show them, which is a colder reason than the one she started with.

stories.situation: Fundação Pedra Lume donated 60 tablets to the school. They stayed locked in a store cupboard for 7 months, because the donation's insurance clause required one named member of staff to be responsible for loss or damage, and nobody would put their name on the form. The staff talked about the tablets as though they were a problem the foundation had given them.
stories.stakes: The clause made one teacher personally liable, on a municipal salary, for equipment worth more than a year of it. Luana was asking her colleagues to do training on Wednesdays after a full teaching day, for something most of them thought would be taken away again, and she had to ask the diretora to accept a risk the diretora had already refused once.
actions: Read the donation agreement properly, which nobody had, and found the liability sat with whoever signed rather than with the school
Asked the foundation's programme manager to move the clause to the school as an institution; was refused, and then put her own name on the form
Took the parents' council through it first, because she wanted parents in the room when she went back to the diretora, and the council raised R$ 3,200 for a lockable charging trolley
Ran 6 training sessions of 45 minutes each, built around one lesson each teacher already taught rather than around the devices
Stopped insisting on the shared booking sheet after the second month, when it was clear the teachers were trading slots between themselves and the sheet was only making her the gatekeeper
stories.result: 9 of the school's 14 teachers were using the tablets by the end of the year, 4 days a week between them. Nothing has been lost or broken. Her name is still on the form. The cluster's other 4 schools copied the trolley and the Wednesday sessions.
stories.reflection: She thinks she was slow about the real obstacle. She spent two months making the case for tablets in lessons when the obstacle was a sentence in a contract and the fact that nobody wanted to be blamed. She goes looking for the paperwork first now.

stories.nickname: The app I talked everyone into
stories.situation: In her first year as technology coordinator, Luana brought in a maths practice app from Trilho Educação and ran it as a pilot in 7 of the school's 14 classes, 210 children. She had used it with her own class, liked it, and did not ask the families anything before starting. Each child needed a login, and the app expected a working connection at home for the practice set.
stories.stakes: She had spent the credit from the tablets to get the teachers to agree, and had told the foundation the pilot would be the evidence for a bigger grant. Four of the seven teachers had only agreed because she asked them to.
actions: Watched the usage fall for 5 months while telling herself it was the start-of-year workload
Printed a survey and sent it home with every child, got 118 families back, and found 62% had no connection at home they could rely on for homework
Took the figures to the pilot teachers before she took them to the foundation, and said plainly that she had not asked anyone before she started
Wrote to the foundation and asked them to stop the pilot rather than let it run out the year, which cost the school the bigger grant
Rebuilt the practice sets as printed sheets generated from the app's own question bank, which the 7 classes still use
stories.result: Logins went from 71% of the children in the first week to 9% by the twelfth. The pilot was stopped at her request and the grant went elsewhere. The printed sheets stayed, and the survey is now the first thing the cluster does before any device project.
stories.reflection: She had asked the teachers and not the families, because the teachers were the ones she needed to say yes. She had the habit of counting and did not use it until the thing had already failed. The 118 forms took an afternoon; she could have done them in February.

stories.situation: Luana's grandmother, Dona Neusa, ran a sewing workshop out of the garage with 4 seamstresses, making school uniforms for shops in the neighbourhood. She could read but wrote slowly and hated doing it, so from the age of 11 Luana kept the books: who finished what, how many pieces, what was owed on Friday, in school exercise books because that is what was in the house.
stories.stakes: The money in the exercise books was the household's money, and three of the four seamstresses were paid out of it by the piece. A column added up wrong meant somebody was short that week, and Luana would be the one who had to tell them.
actions: Kept the piece counts and the Friday payments, 9 exercise books over the years, and checked the total twice because her grandmother would not
Worked out at 14 that the uniform skirts were being sold at a rate that did not cover the second fitting, and argued the rate up to R$ 2.40 a piece
Took over the quoting for new shop orders from then on, which her grandmother never asked her to do and never mentioned
Kept the books going through secondary school and handed them to her cousin when she started university
stories.result: The workshop ran until her grandmother's hands gave out. Luana can still say what the Friday total was in a given month. She has never since worked anywhere that counted anything as carefully as that garage did.
stories.reflection: She did not think of it as anything until an interviewer asked her where she learned to count things. It is also where she learned that the person doing the work usually knows the number and nobody has ever asked them for it.

stories.nickname: The year of the Tuesday appointments
stories.situation: Luana's mother was diagnosed with breast cancer in her first year of teaching. The treatment ran 14 months and 23 chemotherapy sessions, and Luana took her to every one, which meant two buses each way and a Tuesday that started at half past four in the morning.
stories.stakes: She was in her probation year at the school and told nobody for the first weeks, because a teacher on probation who asks for anything can be moved to another school. Her mother would not go to the sessions alone and there was no one else to take her.
actions: Told the diretora eventually, and asked for her Tuesday timetable to be rearranged rather than for time off
Turned down the coordination post when it came up that year and did not explain why, which she now thinks was a mistake
Kept the Friday planning for the class ahead by a fortnight, so a supply teacher could walk in on a Tuesday and teach from the folder
Missed 4 days of teaching across the whole 14 months
Said yes when two colleagues offered to cover, which she had not done before and found harder than the hospital
stories.result: Her mother has been clear for four years and goes to the Roda de Sábado meetings now to help with the coffee. Luana got the coordination post when it came round again. The fortnight-ahead planning folder is still how she works.
stories.reflection: She had thought asking for help was the same as being found out. It was the two colleagues who covered, not the hospital, that changed how she works, and she is aware that she only learned it because she ran out of room to do otherwise.

stories.situation: Teachers in Luana's district were each making the same worksheets alone on Sunday nights and had nowhere to say so. She asked 6 teachers to a bakery on a Saturday morning, with the rule that everyone brought one thing they had made and one thing that had gone wrong that week.
stories.stakes: Nothing was at stake, which is why it survived. Three of the first 6 came because she had asked them personally and would not have come otherwise, and if the second meeting had been four people the thing would have died there.
actions: Kept the format fixed and short, 2 hours on the last Saturday of the month, and never moved it, so people stopped asking whether it was on
Set up a shared folder so what was brought to the room did not stay in the room; it holds 312 lesson sheets now
Put the teachers who were quiet in the room in charge of one part of the session, which is how two of the current organisers started
Handed the running of it to 3 teachers in rotation and took her own name off the group description
stories.result: 140 teachers across 11 schools are in it. She has not led a session for 5 months and has been to the last two as an ordinary attender. Two of the state's other districts have asked how it works.
stories.reflection: Her first instinct was to make it bigger, and the thing that made it last was keeping it the same. She also knows she gave it away partly because running it had started to be the part of her week she was proudest of, which is not a good reason to keep hold of something.

stories.nickname: Ten minutes in a room with no teachers in it
stories.situation: After the pilot was stopped, Trilho Educação invited Luana to their office to talk about what had happened. She sat in on the planning meeting afterwards, and watched 3 people decide in about 10 minutes to drop the offline mode from the next release, for a product that was in 1,400 schools. Nobody in the room had taught. Nobody asked what share of those schools looked like hers.
stories.stakes: She had the survey in her bag and did not say anything, because she had been invited as a guest and did not know whether she was allowed to. The decision went out to every school on the platform.
actions: Asked afterwards, in the corridor, how they decided, and was told honestly that offline was 4% of sessions
Worked out that 4% of sessions was not 4% of schools, and wrote it up with her 118 survey forms as the only evidence she had
Sent it to the two people from the meeting; one replied, and the offline mode stayed in the release that followed
Started asking, at every supplier meeting since, who in the room has been in a classroom this year
stories.result: The offline mode stayed. She was asked to sit on the company's teacher panel, unpaid, and has been in 4 of their product sessions since. It is the first time anything she wrote changed something outside her own district.
stories.reflection: The decision was not careless, it was made on the only number they had. She wants to be the person in that room who has the other number, and she does not want to be the teacher they invite as a guest to be nice. That is the whole reason she is applying.

goals.shortTerm: Product or implementation at an education technology company selling to public school systems in Brazil, owning the part that meets teachers: what a classroom can actually run, how a rollout is trained, what gets measured. Not a teacher-relations job that sits outside the product decisions.
goals.longTerm: To run the schools-facing side of a company that sells to Brazilian state education secretariats, with the authority to stop a release that will not work in a school without a reliable connection. Later, the other side of that table, inside a secretariat.
goals.planB: Back into the municipal system as a district technology coordinator, or onto the education programme team at a foundation like the one that donated the tablets, where she would at least be near the money decisions.
goals.whyMba: She can read a classroom and she can count things nobody has thought to count. She has never held a budget, priced anything or read a contract, and she cannot explain how a company that sells to a state secretariat makes money, which means she cannot tell a good product decision from a cheap one.
goals.whyNow: Six years in, the coordination post is as far as the municipal scale goes without leaving teaching for administration. Her mother is well. Roda de Sábado runs without her. The teacher panel got her into the rooms where decisions are made and showed her she cannot follow the conversation.

redFlags: GMAT 650 with Q42 is below the median at her target schools
No business experience at all: no budget, no P&L, no commercial contract, no private-sector employer
Six years entirely on charity and municipal salary scales, which makes her post-MBA salary expectations hard to read
Quantitative readiness: no mathematics beyond secondary school, and a 40-hour online course as the only formal preparation
Employer and university will be unrecognisable to an admissions reader, with no external ranking to anchor them
No international experience beyond one self-funded week in Montevideo, and English is a working language she learned at evening class
